messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 70
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 71

She is seventy now, elegant even in the way she sits down, with a silk scarf knotted neatly at her throat and careful lipstick that never quite hides how tired she is. She has been a fashion designer for most of her adult life, and she still speaks about fabric the way some people speak about music—how weight changes movement, how color changes mood, how a seam can hold or fail under pressure. Before the trauma, she remembers herself as busy, social, and sure of her eye. She ran a small atelier with her husband, taking private clients and altering gowns late into the night before weddings and galas. She liked the rhythm of the work, the intimacy of fitting strangers into versions of themselves they wanted the world to see.

The event she returns to happened eight years ago, on an ordinary afternoon that now feels to her like the dividing line in her life. She was leaving the studio after meeting with a client and walking toward her car in a crowded commercial district. She remembers hearing shouting first, sharp and angry, and turning before she understood what she was seeing. A young man was attacking another man on the sidewalk. At first she thought it was a fight that would break apart in seconds, but then she saw the weapon, saw the victim fall, saw the attacker keep going while people screamed and scattered. She froze. She says this with shame, though at the time she felt as if her body had turned to stone. The sounds come back to her most vividly—the wet impact, a woman crying, someone yelling for help in Spanish and then in English, sirens that seemed to take far too long. She remembers the victim’s hand twitching near the curb and a single shoe lying in the street. Even now, these details arrive with terrible clarity.

In the days afterward, she tells herself she should be grateful she was not physically harmed. Friends say exactly that. But she does not feel grateful; she feels shaken open. She cannot stop seeing the scene when she closes her eyes. The first nights, she startles awake drenched in sweat, convinced she hears shouting outside the bedroom window. Her husband reaches for her and she jerks away before she knows it is him. During the day, she tries to return to work, but when a client drops a metal hanger and it clatters against the floor, her heart races so hard she has to sit down. She begins avoiding the street where it happened, then the entire neighborhood, then any crowded shopping area. She insists that clients come to the atelier by appointment only. She no longer goes alone to buy fabric.

She also begins to change in ways that trouble her more quietly. She has always drawn inspiration from people watching—from movement, posture, the life of a city—but now she studies exits when she enters a room. She notices hands, tempers, distances between bodies. She distrusts strangers reflexively and feels angry at herself for it. A part of her mind is always scanning. If someone raises his voice on the street, she crosses immediately. If she sees two men arguing, her chest tightens and her legs weaken. She tells herself, this is ridiculous, you are an old woman, you should know better, but her body does not listen.

Her work narrows with her life. She still designs, but more from home, sketching in the quiet morning hours when she feels least agitated. She used to love flowing red fabrics; now she finds herself avoiding that color without fully admitting why. When clients ask for dramatic details—sharp slashes, asymmetry, distressed textures—she feels an odd resistance, as if beauty has become entangled with violence. She grows less patient during fittings. If someone stands too suddenly behind her, she gasps and presses a hand to her chest. She laughs it off, embarrassed, but afterward she feels depleted. Sometimes she loses track of what a client has just said because, for a few seconds, she is no longer in her studio but back on the sidewalk, staring at that fallen body and unable to move.

Her husband has become both companion and witness to the shrinking of her world. He invites her to dinners she used to enjoy, gallery openings, family baptisms, street festivals with music she once loved. She declines more often than not. Crowds feel dangerous; even celebrations feel unpredictable. Their grandchildren run and shriek during visits, and although she adores them, the sudden noise sends a jolt through her. She slips into the kitchen to breathe, ashamed that joy can sound to her like alarm. At night she checks the locks more than once. If her husband is late coming home, she imagines catastrophe instantly and cannot settle until she hears his key in the door.

What troubles her most in the present is not only fear but the sense that the world has become morally unstable. She witnessed a stranger’s life end in broad daylight while others watched, helpless and horrified, and since then ordinary life has never fully regained its innocence. She says she still knows how to drape silk over a form, how to pin a hem, how to make something beautiful with her hands. But inside, she lives as if terrible things can erupt at any moment. Even in safety, some part of her remains on that sidewalk, listening for shouting, waiting for the next blow.
